accepted.s: The Electricity Act, 2003 was notified on which date?
accepted.x: The Electricity Act, 2003 was notified on 10 June 2003.
accepted.tq: Use the precise date rather than the year alone.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of the Electricity Act, 2003?
accepted.x: The Act introduced or facilitated electricity trading; it did not abolish it. It also delicensed generation, required unbundling of SEBs and introduced open access and SERCs.
accepted.tq: Find the option that reverses a major provision of the Act.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Electricity Act, 2003:
1. It consolidates laws relating to generation, transmission, distribution and trading of electricity.
2. It established the Central Electricity Authority, regulatory commissions and an appellate tribunal.
3. It required State Electricity Boards to remain fully integrated.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Act required SEBs to be unbundled.
accepted.tq: Identify the statement that reverses the unbundling provision.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s:
Which of the following bodies are statutory bodies under the Ministry of Power?
1. Central Electricity Authority
2. Appellate Tribunal for Electricity
3. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: CEA, APTEL and CERC are statutory bodies under the Ministry of Power.
accepted.tq: Use the all-inclusive option when every listed body belongs to the same group.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s: The Andhra Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission was established under which legislation?
accepted.x: APERC was set up under the AP Electricity Reform Act, 1998.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the state reform legislation from the later central Electricity Act.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s: After the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh, APERC served both successor States for a period of
accepted.x: Following bifurcation, APERC served both States for up to six months under the AP Reorganisation Act.
accepted.tq: Test the exact transitional period attached to reorganisation.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s: The Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020 primarily provide for
o: allocation of coal to thermal plants
time limits for new connections and service standards
accepted.x: The 2020 Rules prescribe time limits for new electricity connections and service standards for consumers.
accepted.tq: Match the consumer-rights rules with their service-delivery function.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s: With reference to renewable energy under the Electricity Act, 2003, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: CEA asked Parliament to be treated as the Central Government.
MNRE asked a parliamentary committee to be treated as the Central Government.
APERC was treated as the Central Government by the Act.
CERC asked a parliamentary committee to be treated as the Central Government.
accepted.x: MNRE asked a parliamentary committee to be treated as the “Central Government” for renewables under the Act.
accepted.tq: Use the who-requested-what formulation to distinguish authorities.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Body)
a. CERC
a. SERCs
c. APTEL
d. CEA
List-II (Function or feature)
i. Reports on installed capacity and National Electricity Plan
 ii. Central tariffs and inter-State matters
 iii. State retail tariffs, licensing and standards
 iv. Appeals against CERC and SERC orders
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: CERC handles central tariffs and inter-State matters; SERCs handle State retail tariffs and licensing; APTEL hears appeals; CEA publishes technical power-sector reports.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes with mismatched regulatory functions.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission?
o: It fixes retail tariffs for all consumer classes in every State.
It deals with central tariffs and inter-State matters and regulates power exchanges such as IEX.
It is a non-statutory body under the Ministry of Finance.
It hears appeals against orders of all courts in electricity matters.
accepted.x: CERC deals with central tariffs and inter-State matters and regulates power exchanges such as IEX. SERCs generally fix State retail tariffs.
accepted.tq: Separate central and State regulatory jurisdictions.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about State Electricity Regulatory Commissions:
1. Their members are appointed by the State Government.
2. They fix retail tariffs for all consumer classes.
3. They can license, enforce standards and settle disputes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements correctly describe the functions or composition of SERCs.
accepted.tq: Check whether all listed functions belong to the State-level regulator.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s: The Appellate Tribunal for Electricity was established on
accepted.x: APTEL was established on 24 August 2004.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the establishment date of the appellate body from the Act’s notification date.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity?
o: Regulates only renewable-energy exchanges; its Chairperson is the Union Finance Minister.
Publishes the National Electricity Plan; its Chairperson heads the CEA.
Fixes retail tariffs in all States; its Chairperson is appointed by a State Government.
Hears appeals against CERC and SERC orders; its Chairperson is usually a retired Supreme Court judge.
accepted.x: APTEL hears appeals against CERC and SERC orders, and its Chairperson is usually a retired Supreme Court judge.
accepted.tq: Use the body-function-authority combination to reject swapped roles.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s:
Which of the following is the correct chronological order of the following developments?
A. Establishment of CERC
B. Notification of the Electricity Act, 2003
C. Establishment of APTEL
D. Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020
accepted.x: CERC was set up in 1998, the Electricity Act was notified in 2003, APTEL was established in 2004, and the Consumer Rules were issued in 2020.
accepted.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the two intervening dates.
accepted.sec: Electricity Act 2003 - unbundling, open access, regulators

accepted.s:
Which of the following are recognised power exchanges in India?
1. Indian Energy Exchange
2. Power Exchange India Limited
3. Hindustan Power Exchange
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: IEX, PXIL and HPX are the power exchanges identified in the electricity market framework.
accepted.tq: Use the complete-list option when all three named exchanges belong to the group.
accepted.sec: Power markets - exchanges, GDAM, RTM, LPS Rules

accepted.s: The Real-Time Market in the Indian electricity market was introduced in
accepted.x: The Real-Time Market started in 2020.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the adjacent years of RTM and GDAM.
accepted.sec: Power markets - exchanges, GDAM, RTM, LPS Rules

accepted.s: The Green Day-Ahead Market was introduced in
accepted.x: The Green Day-Ahead Market started in 2021.
accepted.tq: Use the one-year sequence between RTM and GDAM.
accepted.sec: Power markets - exchanges, GDAM, RTM, LPS Rules

accepted.s: The Electricity (Late Payment Surcharge and Related Matters) Rules, 2022 enable discoms to
o: fix tariffs without approval of the regulator
obtain free power from renewable generators
clear old dues in instalments and face restriction of power-exchange access for defaulting entities
accepted.x: The 2022 Rules permit discoms to clear old dues in instalments and provide for cutting power-exchange access for defaulters.
accepted.tq: Apply the rule to a defaulting discom rather than confuse it with tariff regulation.
accepted.sec: Power markets - exchanges, GDAM, RTM, LPS Rules

accepted.s: The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme, which funds smart prepaid meters, was launched in
accepted.x: RDSS was launched in 2021 and provides funding for smart prepaid meters and distribution-system improvements.
accepted.tq: Test the launch year of the scheme separately from the year of the surcharge rules.
accepted.sec: Smart prepaid metering rollout

accepted.s: The amount sanctioned to Andhra Pradesh under the RDSS for smart metering and grid modernisation was
accepted.x: Andhra Pradesh was sanctioned ₹15,083.14 crore for smart metering and grid modernisation.
accepted.tq: Read the exact quantitative figure, including the decimal component.
accepted.sec: Smart prepaid metering rollout

accepted.s: Energy Statistics (India) is published by
o: Energy Institute of the United Kingdom
National Statistics Office, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
Central Electricity Authority, Ministry of Power
accepted.x: Energy Statistics (India) is published by the CSO, now the National Statistics Office, under MoSPI.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the national statistical publication from power-sector and international reports.
accepted.sec: Energy data publications - publisher  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which one of the following publications is correctly matched with its publisher?
o: World Energy Outlook — Central Electricity Authority
Statistical Review of World Energy — International Energy Agency
World Energy Outlook — International Energy Agency
accepted.x: The World Energy Outlook is published by the International Energy Agency in Paris. The Statistical Review of World Energy is published by the Energy Institute.
accepted.tq: Identify the publication whose publisher is correctly paired rather than swapping international agencies.
accepted.sec: Energy data publications - publisher  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The Statistical Review of World Energy is published by the
o: Energy Institute of the United Kingdom
accepted.x: The Statistical Review of World Energy is published by the Energy Institute of the UK; it was formerly associated with BP.
accepted.tq: Use the publisher’s institutional identity, not the former publisher’s name.
accepted.sec: Energy data publications - publisher  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
Which of the following publications are associated with NITI Aayog?
1. India Energy Security Scenarios 2047
2. Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero
3. National Electricity Plan
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: NITI Aayog is associated with India Energy Security Scenarios 2047 and the 2026 Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero. The National Electricity Plan is a CEA report.
accepted.tq: Reject the statement that assigns a CEA publication to NITI Aayog.
accepted.sec: Energy data publications - publisher  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly represents per capita electricity generation in 2024?
o: India 1,418 kWh; China 7,097 kWh; USA 12,701 kWh
India 1,460 kWh; China 8,000 kWh; USA 12,701 kWh
India 1,418 kWh; China 12,701 kWh; USA 7,097 kWh
India 7,097 kWh; China 1,418 kWh; USA 12,701 kWh
accepted.x: In 2024, per capita generation was 1,418 kWh in India, 7,097 kWh in China and 12,701 kWh in the USA.
accepted.tq: Keep the country-value pairs together while eliminating swapped figures.
accepted.sec: Per capita electricity consumption - India vs world, states, HDI  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which statement best explains the link between per capita electricity consumption and HDI-oriented energy policy?
o: Per capita electricity consumption is unrelated to energy use and well-being.
Energy policy focuses only on electricity exports and not on domestic well-being.
A higher HDI necessarily requires electricity consumption to fall below the minimum level.
Per capita electricity consumption is treated as a proxy for all energy use, and a minimum level is needed for acceptable well-being.
accepted.x: Per capita electricity consumption is used as a proxy for overall energy use, and a certain minimum consumption is considered necessary for acceptable well-being.
accepted.tq: Apply the indicator concept to the policy objective instead of treating it as a simple output measure.
accepted.sec: Per capita electricity consumption - India vs world, states, HDI  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Approximately what proportion of India’s energy use is electricity?
accepted.x: Only about one-fifth of India’s energy use is electricity.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the share of electricity in total energy use from electricity’s share in generation.
accepted.sec: Per capita electricity consumption - India vs world, states, HDI  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: India is the world’s ____ largest producer of electricity.
accepted.x: India is the third-largest electricity producer in the world.
accepted.tq: Test the global rank directly without confusing production with renewable capacity.
accepted.sec: India's global rank - generation, consumption, renewables  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: India’s electricity generation increased from 1,020.2 billion units in 2013–14 to approximately how much in 2024–25?
accepted.x: Electricity generation rose from 1,020.2 BU in 2013–14 to 1,830 BU in 2024–25.
accepted.tq: Use the two-endpoint comparison and identify the later value.
accepted.sec: India's global rank - generation, consumption, renewables  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly states India’s recent global positions in renewable energy?
o: Third in renewable capacity, fourth in wind and third in solar
Third in renewable capacity, second in wind and fourth in solar
Fifth in renewable capacity, fourth in wind and third in solar
Fourth in renewable capacity, third in wind and fifth in solar
accepted.x: The recent figures place India third in renewable capacity, fourth in wind and third in solar.
accepted.tq: Keep the three rankings in their respective categories and avoid cross-swapping them.
accepted.sec: India's global rank - generation, consumption, renewables  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Solar power was the world’s second-largest growth market in
accepted.x: Solar was the second-largest growth market in 2025.
accepted.tq: Separate the market-growth year from the renewable-ranking years.
accepted.sec: India's global rank - generation, consumption, renewables  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which statement correctly describes the older and newer figures relating to India’s renewable-energy rankings?
o: Older figures placed India third in renewable energy and fourth in solar; newer figures place it fifth in both.
Older figures placed India fifth in renewable energy and third in solar; newer figures place it fourth in both.
Older figures placed India fourth in renewable energy and fifth in solar; newer figures place it third in renewable capacity and third in solar.
The ranking remained unchanged at fourth in renewable energy and fifth in solar.
accepted.x: Older figures cited fourth in renewable energy and fifth in solar, while newer figures cite third in renewable capacity and third in solar; another recent source also reports fourth for renewable capacity, reflecting the stated source variation.
accepted.tq: Track changing rankings by separating older and newer reference figures.
accepted.sec: India's global rank - generation, consumption, renewables  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Under the Updated Nationally Determined Contribution of August 2022, India committed to reducing the emissions intensity of GDP by what percentage by 2030 from the 2005 level?
accepted.x: The Updated NDC set a target of reducing GDP emissions intensity by 45% by 2030 from the 2005 level.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the emissions-intensity target from the non-fossil-capacity target.
accepted.sec: Non-fossil share vs Panchamrit / NDC  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. India achieved the 50% non-fossil installed-capacity target five years ahead of 2030.
2. The target was achieved in June 2025.
3. Emissions intensity had already declined by 36%.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct: the 50% target was achieved in June 2025, five years early, and emissions intensity had declined by 36%.
accepted.tq: Use the all-inclusive option when the achievement, timing and supporting indicator all agree.
accepted.sec: Non-fossil share vs Panchamrit / NDC  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: India’s share of non-fossil installed capacity was reported as 51.93% in December 2025 and more than ____ in August 2026.
accepted.x: The share was 51.93% in December 2025 and exceeded 54% in August 2026.
accepted.tq: Read the time-linked progression and distinguish an exact percentage from a greater-than figure.
accepted.sec: Non-fossil share vs Panchamrit / NDC  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT a Panchamrit commitment announced in the context of COP26?
o: 45% reduction in GDP emissions intensity by 2030 from the 2005 level
50% of energy needs from renewables by 2030
accepted.x: The 45% emissions-intensity reduction is an Updated NDC target. Panchamrit includes 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, 50% energy from renewables by 2030 and Net Zero by 2070.
accepted.tq: Separate the Panchamrit commitments from the later Updated NDC targets.
accepted.sec: Non-fossil share vs Panchamrit / NDC  [GROUP-II]
